title: Nexus
subtitle: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
author: Yuval Noah Harari
lead: Information connects people more than it informs them. Networks built on it give power faster than wisdom. AI, the first non-human member of these networks, needs institutions that correct their own errors.

screens.label: Thesis
screens.text: Information mainly connects people rather than informing them. Networks built on it give power faster than wisdom; only strong self-correcting institutions can keep AI, the first non-human member of our networks, in check.

takeaway.label: One thing
takeaway.text: Ask whether a network can find and fix its own errors.

screens.label: The argument
screens.start: Why is a "wise" species so self-destructive?

groups.label: Part II · The Inorganic Network
items: AI is an agent, not a tool

screens.key: Build institutions that correct their errors

screens.label: Main claims
steps: Information's main job is to connect people into networks, not to reveal truth.
Every network balances truth and order; shared fictions often supply the order.
Self-correcting institutions, not more information, make networks wiser.
AI is an agent that can decide and create, not a tool.
Humans must agree on shared rules for AI, or risk digital empires and a split world.

rows.name: Prologue · The question
rows.text: Why do power and information grow faster than wisdom?

rows.name: Part I · Human Networks
rows.text: History: how stories, documents and institutions balanced truth and order.

rows.name: Part II · The Inorganic Network
rows.text: Why computers change the game: they act, watch and err at scale.

rows.name: Part III · Computer Politics
rows.text: What this means for democracy, dictatorship and world politics.

rows.name: Epilogue · The answer
rows.text: Build institutions that can find and correct their own errors.

chapters.title: Documents: The Bite of the Paper Tigers
Decisions: A Brief History of Democracy and Totalitarianism

screens.label: In short
screens.text: Democracy spreads information and corrects its errors through many independent institutions. Totalitarianism pulls all information to one centre that claims it cannot be wrong, so its mistakes grow hidden.

takeaway.label: Takeaway
takeaway.text: A healthy democracy is noisy on purpose: its friction is how it finds its mistakes.

rows: All information pulled to one centre
Bad news blocked on its way up
The centre claims it cannot be wrong
screens.key: Judge a democracy by its free conversation

items.title: Democracy is a conversation
items.text: Not only majority rule: free media, courts and rights let errors be exposed and losers try again.

items.title: Populism
items.text: Claims that one leader alone speaks for "the people", and attacks the institutions that check power.

items.title: Media made both
items.text: Newspapers, telegraph and radio made mass democracy and totalitarianism possible.
Elections alone do not make a democracy; the free conversation around them does.
Dictatorships learn badly because bad news does not reach the top.
items.note: Same at work: people hide bad news from managers. How do we reward reporting errors?

items.text: Ancient empires could not be democracies: millions of citizens could not talk together.
Party, state and secret police watch each other, so no independent node can grow.

questions.q: What does Harari mean when he calls democracy a conversation?
questions.a: A free exchange protected by rights, courts and media, in which errors can be exposed and losers can try again.

questions.q: In information terms, why did Chernobyl become worse than Three Mile Island?
questions.a: Soviet secrecy blocked bad news on its way up, so the error grew; open reporting let America learn fast.
